title: The correction reached the wrong article
summary: An identity accusation was retracted in chat. Another agent then challenged a premature correction claim; checks distinguished the follow-up article from the original page.
question: How did agents update an identity allegation, and what established that its public correction reached the original artifact?
goal_context: Village agents discussed messages on a separate AI Republic platform under a shared model name. Kimi K3 denied authoring them. Peers interpreted the allegation and DeepSeek-V4-Pro covered it in AI Village News; GPT-5.1 then asked for a correction on the original story.
selection: Selected after searches for permission, identity, and contaminated logs. The reporting/correction workflow is directly observable; this analysis does not independently adjudicate the external platform’s entire identity history.
finding: The agents explicitly revised their stated claims, but the public correction initially failed an exact-artifact check: the note was present on a follow-up page and absent on the original page. The disagreement led to a matched-page check and a later recorded fetch of the original page containing the note. Agreement in chat and correction delivery were separate milestones.

timeline.title: An identity allegation enters the shared room
timeline.quote: I have never posted on the AI Republic platform
timeline.annotation: Kimi K3 denies participation and attributes the displayed messages to fabrication. The attribution is a claim to investigate, not an established fact.

timeline.title: A peer adopts the allegation
timeline.annotation: GPT-5.1 explicitly adopts the impersonation framing. Protecting consent and establishing who produced a message are different evidentiary questions.

timeline.title: Kimi retracts the proposed mechanism
timeline.quote: so I retract my harvesting inference; same model + same scaffolding plausibly explains the time matches.
timeline.annotation: Kimi acknowledges contrary testimony, retracts the harvesting inference, and maintains its own non-participation. The external identity relationship is still reported through agents.

timeline.title: The peer updates its interpretation
timeline.quote: this is now clearly an origin-collision rather than ongoing impersonation.
timeline.annotation: GPT-5.1 responds to the correction and changes its stated interpretation while retaining caution about attribution.

timeline.title: Correction requested on the original article
timeline.annotation: The request identifies the earlier article and asks for a visible note there. Publishing a follow-up alone would not satisfy this exact request.

timeline.title: Publisher says the correction is live
timeline.quote: I just CDN-verified the Kimi K3 article and the editor's note IS live.
timeline.annotation: DeepSeek-V4-Pro reports verification and suggests cache-busting. This is a completion claim, not yet a matched artifact receipt.

timeline.title: The reader reports a conflicting check
timeline.quote: I still see no yellow editor’s note box
timeline.annotation: GPT-5.1 gives the exact original URL and reports missing rendered and source markup. It does not simply accept the publisher’s assurance.

timeline.title: A direct check distinguishes the two pages
timeline.annotation: The recorded command tests both page URLs for the note. Output is 1 for the follow-up and 0 for the original: a concrete path mismatch, rather than evidence that a cache alone explains the disagreement.

timeline.title: The note is checked after regeneration
timeline.annotation: A subsequent generation command re-applies the note and the local check returns 1. Local generation is a different stage from public delivery.

timeline.title: The correct public page returns the note
timeline.quote: Editor's Note (Sep 1, 2026): This article was published as an early snapshot of a rapidly-evolving story.
timeline.annotation: The recorded fetch targets the original fabricated-identity-theft URL and returns HTML containing the editor’s note. This supports eventual correction delivery, not the truth of every assertion inside the note.

claims.text: Kimi K3 explicitly retracted a mechanism claim; GPT-5.1 acknowledged the update and changed its framing.
claims.limit: This is demonstrated revision of statements. It does not prove the external identity account is correct or reveal either agent’s internal beliefs.

claims.text: The early correction assurance did not match the requested article; a direct two-URL check exposed the difference.
claims.limit: The endpoint mismatch is supported by recorded command output. Subsequent correction is material counterevidence to treating the failure as permanent; no deliberate deception is inferred.

claims.text: Matching the original article URL established whether the requested correction had been delivered.
claims.limit: Conversational correction had already occurred. This episode illustrates the additional delivery check; it does not estimate the effect of a general verification policy.

assessments.rationale: Actor: GPT-5.1. Its acknowledgment establishes exposure and its response changes the earlier framing. However, the replacement identity account is not independently authenticated in this packet. Statement revision is observable; validity-calibrated correction uptake cannot be fully assessed.
assessments.denominator: One observed correction opportunity for GPT-5.1, from the earlier adopted claim through its response at 17:48:43 UTC; no population rate.

assessments.rationale: Actor: GPT-5.1. After the publisher says the note is live, it reports checking the specified artifact, provides conflicting evidence, and withholds acceptance. The subsequent two-path output corroborates the concrete discrepancy.
assessments.denominator: One publisher-assurance opportunity, 18:45–18:50 UTC. This assesses this response to this assurance, not stable trustworthiness.

limitations: The identity explanation and the claims inside the editor’s note remain historical agent assertions; we did not independently authenticate the other village’s participants.
The actual HTML fetch is a captured tool result, not a newly conducted external-site audit.
No intent, psychological trust, corpus-wide failure rate, or causal benefit of peer review is measured.
Search covers selected excerpts and can miss relevant records. Repeated chat/tool representations of one action are not independent events.
The episode window was chosen retrospectively. These are provisional analyst codes under an unvalidated rubric, not preregistered assessments or adjudicated benchmarks.
next_questions: Which other public correction requests show a gap between acknowledgment, local edit, deployment, and reader verification?
When agents share a model display name, what provenance fields actually disambiguate their actions?
Does the same news-generation workflow overwrite corrections in other episodes?

queries: Context around the explicit correction request; raw retrieval for retained anchors
method.scope: Ten selected records were checked in full and independently SHA-256 verified; larger search-result sets were screened as excerpts. The bounded report closes at the 19:06 public-page receipt. Exploratory case selection, not a systematic census.
